title: Final self-assessment: 40 questions, Modules 1–8
body_md:
## Forty moments, one decision each

A voice on the phone sounds exactly like your cousin, and it wants gift-card numbers right now. This self-assessment is made of moments like that: **40 questions, five from each of Modules 1–8**, each asking what you would infer or do in a concrete situation. Some of the messages are plausible and perfectly legitimate, so spotting pressure is a cue to verify, not proof of a crime. Choose one answer per question, and read why every option works or fails before you move on.

### What the result is, and what it is not

The exam is self-paced, untimed and not proctored: no outside assessor, nobody watching, so take your time. The personal benchmark is **80% (32 of 40)**, and you can retake the complete set. Treat the result as a mirror rather than a certificate: it is a personal record kept in this browser, and with optional progress sync an encrypted copy can also be stored remotely. It is **not independently verified**, not issued by a server, not a verified credential, and it proves neither who took the exam nor what you can do in real life.

An earlier pass is preserved separately and does not count toward the current local completion record. For that record, pass this revised exam at 80% or higher. Within this revision, a previous pass may remain after a weaker retake, so judge yourself by the new score.

### Sorting your misses

Afterward, revisit the questions you missed by **decision type**: reading evidence and report denominators (Module 1); pressure and independent contact (2); destination and login route (3); password, MFA and recovery (4); payment and provider response (5); voice, video and provenance (6); device, browser and network limits (7); containment, evidence and recovery (8). Write down one practical change for your own setup. And please do not type real passwords, codes, messages, URLs or payment details into this exam.

### Where the questions come from

The scenarios are invented. The [UK NCSC scam guide](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/phishing-scams/spot-scams), [NIST authenticator standard](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/), [FTC post-scam guidance](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/what-do-if-you-were-scammed) and [C2PA provenance guidance](https://spec.c2pa.org/specifications/specifications/2.4/security/Harms_Modelling.html) were checked on 2026-10-20. UK NCSC advice on breaking contact, NIST authenticator distinctions, FTC US consumer payment and recovery guidance, and C2PA provenance limits inform the questions. Reporting and payment rights depend on your country and provider, and no source certifies this assessment.

questions.question: A report says “10,000 scam complaints last year.” What can you reasonably conclude from that figure?

choices.text: Your own chance of being scammed this year is 10,000 divided by the country’s population.
choices.explanation: A count of complaints is not a population survey, so it cannot give any one person’s odds.

choices.text: Exactly 10,000 people were scammed last year, one complaint per victim.
choices.explanation: One person may file several reports, and many victims never file any.

choices.text: It shows 10,000 complaints were filed, not how many people were scammed.
choices.explanation: It counts only those who reported, and the reports themselves may not have been checked.

questions.question: A message arrives through a channel you rarely use and gives almost no context. What should drive your first decision?

choices.text: Trust it if it greets you by your full name, since a stranger would not have that.
choices.explanation: Names are easy to come by and do not show who is really behind the sender.

choices.text: Treat anything that arrives by a channel you rarely use as fraud, and delete it unread.
choices.explanation: Legitimate services use new channels too, so the channel alone settles nothing.

choices.text: Identify what it asks you to do, and verify any important claim by a route you already know.
choices.explanation: The channel alone does not diagnose fraud; the requested action and an independent check are what count.

questions.question: A stranger builds a friendship with you, then introduces a private investing site. Which pattern deserves the closest check?

choices.text: A relationship-based investment fraud pattern.
choices.explanation: Trust built first and a private investment offered second is the pattern to check for, though it is a reason to verify, not proof about this particular person.

choices.text: A state-directed intelligence operation aimed at recruiting you.
choices.explanation: Nothing in the story points to a state actor.

choices.text: A one-off scam built around a parcel that never arrives.
choices.explanation: Nothing in the story involves a shipment or a sale.

choices.text: A routine account-recovery request from a service you use.
choices.explanation: What is on offer is an investment, not a way back into an account.

questions.question: An attacker emails accounts payable, posing as the CFO, to redirect a transfer. What is this usually called?

choices.text: Ransomware (files locked for a ransom)
choices.explanation: Ransomware locks or ransoms data, while here the attacker is only changing where a payment goes.

choices.text: Quishing (phishing through a QR code)
choices.explanation: Quishing uses a QR code as the lure, and no QR code appears here.

choices.text: BEC (Business Email Compromise)
choices.explanation: BEC is the umbrella term for email schemes that impersonate executives or suppliers to redirect payments.

choices.text: Credential stuffing (replaying leaked logins)
choices.explanation: Credential stuffing replays reused logins against sign-in pages and has nothing to do with a payment instruction.

questions.question: A video meeting shows several executives you know asking for a large transfer. Which control is strongest?

choices.text: Study the faces for lip-sync errors and glitches, and approve the transfer if you find none.
choices.explanation: A video with no visible flaws still gives nobody the authority to order a payment.

choices.text: Pause, and confirm this exact transaction through a separate contact and the usual approvals.
choices.explanation: That check works whether the video is fake or an account has been compromised.

choices.text: Ask the executives to confirm the transfer in writing, in the meeting chat itself.
choices.explanation: The same channel, which may be under the attacker’s control, can simply repeat the instruction.

questions.question: A ticket offer says “Only three left; decide in ten minutes.” What does this show?

choices.text: That the seller is a fraud, because any honest seller would let you take your time.
choices.explanation: A genuine sale can be time-limited too.

choices.text: Scarcity and urgency are pressure cues; independently check the seller and terms before paying.
choices.explanation: Limited stock does exist, so the cue calls for verification rather than a verdict.

choices.text: That the seller is genuine, because only a real seller would know exactly how many tickets remain.
choices.explanation: The count on a page can be invented.

questions.question: A suspicious caller arrives with a convincing story, a pretext. What breaks it?

choices.text: Demand the caller’s name and badge number, and write them down.
choices.explanation: A badge number supplied by the same caller is not independent evidence.

choices.text: Stay on the line so that the police can trace the call while you keep them talking.
choices.explanation: Staying connected neither authenticates the caller nor traces them safely.

choices.text: Keep challenging the caller’s story until they contradict themselves.
choices.explanation: Arguing only gives the caller more time to steer you.

choices.text: Hang up and call back on a number you already had for that organization.
choices.explanation: The pretext lives inside the channel the caller controls, so switching channels collapses it.

questions.question: A caller asks you to move money to a “safe account.” Which detail should change your response most?

choices.text: The caller speaks with a noticeable foreign accent.
choices.explanation: An accent says nothing about fraud.

choices.text: The call comes late in the evening, outside business hours.
choices.explanation: Genuine calls can come outside business hours too.

choices.text: The caller can quote the last four digits of your card number.
choices.explanation: Knowing those digits does not authorize a new transfer.

choices.text: The caller insists you stay on the line during the transfer.
choices.explanation: Moving money to a “safe account” at a caller’s direction is the dangerous act, and the demand to stay on the line keeps you from checking. Hang up and verify through your bank by an independent route.

questions.question: A stranger you have chatted with for weeks recommends a small crypto platform and helps you make a successful test withdrawal. Which feature of this story is the strongest sign of the pattern called pig-butchering?

choices.text: Investment returns that sound far too good to be true.
choices.explanation: Unrealistic returns are a warning too, but they are not what defines the pattern in question, which is the move from friendship to platform.

choices.text: They mention that a relative of theirs works at the platform and vouches for it.
choices.explanation: A claimed relative at the platform is social proof nobody has verified.

choices.text: The platform was introduced by someone who spent weeks building rapport.
choices.explanation: Trust-building followed by an investment referral is the warning, and even a small successful withdrawal would not prove the platform safe.

choices.text: They suggest starting with a small amount to see how it goes.
choices.explanation: A small first deposit lowers your guard without validating the site.

questions.question: Which phrase in a live call is enough, by itself, to end the conversation?

choices.text: “Sorry for the noise, I’m calling from a busy open-plan office today.”
choices.explanation: Background noise is not a sign of fraud.

choices.text: “I’ll send you the details by email, so you have everything in writing.”
choices.explanation: Offering details by email does not by itself make a call illegitimate.

choices.text: “Before we start, could you confirm your name for our records, please?”
choices.explanation: Ordinary service calls ask for a name too, though you should still withhold sensitive details from a caller you have not verified.

choices.text: “For your security, install AnyDesk so I can clean your computer remotely.”
choices.explanation: An unsolicited caller who directs you to install remote-access software creates an immediate access risk, so end the call and verify support independently if you need it.

questions.question: Take the fictional address `https://login.paypal.com.account-verify.example/signin`, where .example is a reserved suffix. Which part names the site itself?

choices.text: paypal.com
choices.explanation: The paypal.com you can see sits inside a different host.

choices.text: account-verify.example
choices.explanation: The .example suffix is reserved for examples. Read from the right: in this fictional host, account-verify is the label directly beneath it, and paypal.com appears only in labels to its left. Real suffixes such as co.uk need different parsing.

choices.text: login.paypal.com
choices.explanation: That is only a prefix inside a different host.

choices.text: account-verify.example/signin
choices.explanation: That adds the path, which names a page on the site rather than the site itself.

questions.question: A brand name in a link contains a character that looks like the usual letter but is not. What is the useful response?

choices.text: Use a bookmark or type the known address yourself, then check the real host.
choices.explanation: Look-alike characters make reading an address by eye unreliable, so an independent route is the safer test.

choices.text: Assume any URL with a non-Latin character in it is malicious and close the tab.
choices.explanation: Internationalized domain names can be legitimate.

choices.text: Trust the page if the padlock and HTTPS are showing in the address bar.
choices.explanation: HTTPS protects the connection, not the identity of the business behind it.

questions.question: Your password manager refuses to autofill on a page that looks like your bank’s. What do you do?

choices.text: Stop, open the bank by a saved or independently chosen route, and check the address first.
choices.explanation: A missing autofill is a useful warning rather than proof of phishing, so check the real address and reach the bank by a route you chose yourself.

choices.text: Decide your vault is broken and reset it before touching anything else.
choices.explanation: A fault in the vault is possible, but resetting it before checking the address creates recovery work you may not need.

choices.text: Paste the password in by hand; the bank has probably changed its login flow.
choices.explanation: A real login change is possible, but pasting into this unverified page skips the domain check that autofill was performing.

choices.text: Ignore the missing autofill: you may have private browsing on, which sometimes blocks it.
choices.explanation: Private browsing can affect autofill, but that does not establish the site’s identity.

questions.question: At work, an email asks you to re-enter your payroll credentials. You have not clicked anything. What is the useful way to report it?

choices.text: Delete it quietly; you did not click, so there is nothing worth reporting.
choices.explanation: A report can protect the other people who received it.

choices.text: Forward the live link to every colleague so they can see for themselves that it is fake.
choices.explanation: That spreads a potentially harmful link.

choices.text: Report it through your organization’s phishing-report route, with the message intact.
choices.explanation: The security team can inspect the original, though procedures differ between organizations.

questions.question: A poster by the office copier shows a QR code and says “Your Microsoft 365 password is expiring: scan to renew.” What is the safest move?

choices.text: Scan the code and renew; IT often puts up notices like this one by the printers.
choices.explanation: IT may well post notices, but a poster’s code is not an authenticated route.

choices.text: Ignore the poster, because passwords don’t expire these days.
choices.explanation: Password-expiry rules depend on the organization, and the poster still needs checking.

choices.text: Renew through the SSO portal you already use, and tell IT about the poster.
choices.explanation: A QR code on a wall is the wrong channel for a credential change, since anyone who can walk into the office could have put it up. Use the portal you already trust and warn IT.

choices.text: Scan it, but only carry on if the URL preview on your phone looks plausible.
choices.explanation: A plausible preview can still lead to a destination the attacker controls.

questions.question: A forum you belong to tells you your password was exposed. What is the most useful first move?

choices.text: Change your password on the forum itself, and consider the matter closed.
choices.explanation: The forum needs attention too, but checking for reuse is what stops the same secret opening other accounts.

choices.text: Change it on the forum and everywhere you reused it, important accounts first.
choices.explanation: Fix every account that shares the exposed password, important ones first, and the forum account too; if it was unique, focus on that one account and watch for related exposure.

choices.text: Create a fresh email address and move all your accounts over to it, as a clean start.
choices.explanation: A new address does not remove the exposed password.

choices.text: Wait and see whether your bank or any other service notifies you of anything unusual.
choices.explanation: Waiting for a bank notice leaves any reuse unaddressed.

questions.question: Which MFA tier is phishing-resistant by protocol design?

choices.text: SMS one-time codes sent to your phone
choices.explanation: An SMS code can be intercepted or relayed.

choices.text: TOTP codes from an authenticator app
choices.explanation: A code from an app can be relayed to a phishing page as well.

choices.text: Hardware key or passkey (FIDO2)
choices.explanation: FIDO2 ties the signature to the origin URL, so a fake page cannot produce a valid signature for the real domain.

choices.text: A confirmation link sent to your email
choices.explanation: A confirmation link is not generally tied to the site’s origin the way FIDO2 is.

questions.question: You have added a passkey to one account. What still needs your attention?

choices.text: Nothing about storage, because every passkey is kept in iCloud anyway.
choices.explanation: Where a passkey is stored depends on the platform, the provider and your account setup.

choices.text: Where this passkey is stored, and which recovery methods are still switched on.
choices.explanation: Device-bound and synced passkeys behave differently, and recovery can remain the weaker door.

choices.text: Nothing at all: with a passkey you can never be locked out, so recovery no longer matters.
choices.explanation: You can still lose access, and recovery routes can still be attacked, so both need a plan.

questions.question: Your work account uses an authenticator app, but the recovery phone number on file is no longer yours. What should you do?

choices.text: Send a colleague a screenshot of your backup codes in case you get locked out.
choices.explanation: Backup codes are secrets and must be stored privately.

choices.text: Leave it alone; the authenticator app already protects every route into the account.
choices.explanation: Recovery can bypass the sign-in factor altogether.

choices.text: Update the recovery number through the service or your administrator, and add backups.
choices.explanation: A working recovery route is part of the account’s security.

questions.question: Your password manager flags reused and exposed passwords. Where do you start?

choices.text: Rename your accounts to less guessable usernames so attackers can’t find you.
choices.explanation: Changing usernames does nothing about a secret that is already known or reused.

choices.text: Fix the flagged reused or exposed passwords, important accounts first.
choices.explanation: Start with the flagged passwords on important accounts and then review MFA and recovery, but do not rotate every strong, unique password on a calendar.

choices.text: Delete your old emails so there is less for an attacker to read.
choices.explanation: Deleting mail does not change any account’s credentials.

choices.text: Switch your home Wi-Fi to a hidden network, so outsiders can’t see it.
choices.explanation: Hiding the network name is no remedy for reused passwords.

questions.question: An online store offers a PS5 at 90% off MSRP, payable only by Bitcoin or gift cards, on a domain registered 14 days ago. Which signal is the strongest by itself?

choices.text: The store’s domain was registered only 14 days ago, so it has no track record.
choices.explanation: A new domain deserves a check but is not conclusive by itself.

choices.text: Only gift cards or crypto accepted: payments that are hard to get back.
choices.explanation: Gift-card-or-crypto-only payment at an unfamiliar, steeply discounted store sharply reduces your ordinary dispute options. If you have already paid, ask the gift-card issuer or the crypto exchange or operator promptly about possible recovery, which is not guaranteed; in future, verify the seller and choose a protected payment method if one is offered.

choices.text: The “only 3 left” message nudging you to buy before the stock runs out today.
choices.explanation: Scarcity language is a pressure cue, not proof.

choices.text: The word “sony” in the store’s name, which makes it look like an official reseller.
choices.explanation: A brand word in a store’s name does not prove any affiliation.

questions.question: After you post about a loss, a stranger unexpectedly offers to “recover” your money for a fee. What now?

choices.text: Pay nothing and share nothing; contact the provider you paid through its official route.
choices.explanation: Unsolicited recovery offers tend to compound the loss, while what the provider can do depends on how you paid.

choices.text: Pay the small fee they ask for up front, as a test of whether they can really deliver.
choices.explanation: The fee can be your next loss, and it proves nothing about their ability to recover money.

choices.text: Send the stranger your transaction records and identity documents, so they can start work.
choices.explanation: That exposes more sensitive information without showing that the service is real.

questions.question: An email signed by the “CFO” asks accounts payable to change a vendor’s IBAN before the next invoice is paid. Which control best protects against this payment-redirection fraud?

choices.text: Phone the vendor on a number you already had, and confirm the IBAN change by voice.
choices.explanation: Confirm the exact change with a supplier contact you had on record before the email, and run it through your normal second approval.

choices.text: Check that the sender’s From domain matches the vendor’s real domain exactly.
choices.explanation: A matching From domain can still come from a compromised mailbox.

choices.text: Forward the email to IT for analysis and process the change once they clear it.
choices.explanation: IT analysis can help, but the payment still needs independent confirmation from the supplier.

choices.text: Check that the new IBAN has a valid format for its country and passes validation.
choices.explanation: A well-formed account number can still belong to the wrong recipient.

questions.question: Which payment habits defend best against both physical and digital card skimming?

choices.text: Memorizing your card number and leaving the physical card at home.
choices.explanation: Memorizing a number does not protect it when you type it at a compromised terminal or website.

choices.text: Avoiding online shopping entirely and paying only in person.
choices.explanation: Giving up online shopping does nothing about physical card exposure.

choices.text: Shopping only at small independent stores, because big retailers are the ones that get breached.
choices.explanation: A small store is not inherently safer, and some are careless or fake.

choices.text: Apple Pay or Google Pay where possible, plus virtual cards and instant alerts.
choices.explanation: Where supported, tokenized wallet payments and limited-use virtual cards reduce how often your card number is exposed, and alerts help you detect misuse but do not prevent it.

questions.question: You discover that a bank transfer to a supplier’s changed account details may be fraudulent. What is the first payment-response action?

choices.text: Promise the supplier that the transfer will certainly be reversed, to calm things down.
choices.explanation: A reversal is never guaranteed.

choices.text: Gather absolute proof that it was fraud first, and only then tell the bank, to avoid a false alarm.
choices.explanation: Delay can shrink the payment actions still available.

choices.text: Contact your sending bank’s official fraud channel now and ask about recall, hold or trace.
choices.explanation: The bank needs early notice, and what it can do depends on how the transfer was sent and in which country.

questions.question: Which defensive strategy is the most durable as generative AI keeps improving?

choices.text: Out-of-band verification: callbacks to known numbers, family code words.
choices.explanation: Independent contact and transaction approvals stay useful however convincing fakes become, though a family word is only an extra signal and never sole proof.

choices.text: Training yourself and your family to spot the visual glitches in deepfake video.
choices.explanation: Visible defects may disappear as the tools improve.

choices.text: Avoiding any AI-generated content entirely.
choices.explanation: Avoiding all generated content is not a workable verification process.

choices.text: Trusting AI-text detector tools to flag anything suspicious.
choices.explanation: A detector score cannot authenticate the speaker or authorize a payment.

questions.question: A voice that sounds like your relative urgently asks for gift-card numbers. Which check is best?

choices.text: Trust the voice: you have known it for years, and a stranger could never copy it so well.
choices.explanation: A familiar sound is not authentication, because voices can be cloned.

choices.text: End the call, then reach your relative on a saved number or via a trusted person.
choices.explanation: A voice can be cloned or imitated, and a route you choose yourself tests the story.

choices.text: Ask for a family code word, and if they say it correctly, go ahead and pay.
choices.explanation: A word can leak or be overheard, so it is an aid and never sole authorization.

questions.question: Someone appearing as your CFO on a video call asks for an exceptional payment. Which step protects the decision?

choices.text: Verify it through a separate, known contact and the required payment approvers.
choices.explanation: A separate transaction control survives a manipulated meeting or a compromised account.

choices.text: Ask the “CFO” to confirm in the meeting chat, where the whole team can see the answer.
choices.explanation: The attacker may control that channel too.

choices.text: Pay if the face and voice look and sound flawless, with no artifacts.
choices.explanation: Good picture quality is not authorization.

questions.question: An old friend unexpectedly messages you asking for money. Which check is strongest?

choices.text: Ask a shared-memory question in the same chat, and pay if it is answered.
choices.explanation: The answer may be sitting in the chat history or in public information.

choices.text: Call the saved number or use another established route before deciding.
choices.explanation: Whoever holds a hijacked account can read old chats, so only a separate route shows who is really asking.

choices.text: Run the message through an AI-text detector and pay if it reads as human.
choices.explanation: Writing-style detection does not establish who controls the account or whether the need is real.

questions.question: A viral clip carries valid Content Credentials. What does that establish?

choices.text: That the provenance record validates; the clip’s claims still need independent checking.
choices.explanation: C2PA records where media came from, validated under a trust model, and makes no judgment about whether it is true.

choices.text: That what the clip shows must be true, because its credentials verified without errors.
choices.explanation: Authentic provenance can accompany misleading content.

choices.text: That any clip without credentials must be fake or manipulated, whatever else it shows.
choices.explanation: Legitimate media may simply carry no credentials.

questions.question: A simple flashlight app asks for SMS, contacts and accessibility permissions. What is the best decision?

choices.text: Assume that any accessibility request means the app has complete remote control of the phone.
choices.explanation: The exact powers vary, although this request is still excessive.

choices.text: Grant them: the app store reviews every app before listing it, so it must be safe.
choices.explanation: A store review is no reason to hand over access the app does not need.

choices.text: Decline the unrelated permissions, check the publisher and find a narrower alternative.
choices.explanation: Permissions should fit the app’s function, and what accessibility access can do varies by platform and setting.

questions.question: Your phone loses service unexpectedly, and you also receive an account-recovery notice. What is a proportionate first check?

choices.text: Declare it a confirmed SIM swap straight away, because the phone simply says “No service.”
choices.explanation: That observation does not establish the cause.

choices.text: Contact the carrier and the service by another trusted route, and ask about line changes.
choices.explanation: A SIM takeover is possible, but so is an ordinary outage.

choices.text: Wait a few days and see whether the service comes back by itself before doing anything.
choices.explanation: The recovery notice makes prompt, low-risk checks appropriate.

questions.question: A browser extension asks for access to all websites to do a job you need on only one site. What is the safer choice?

choices.text: Grant access to all sites; legitimate extensions sometimes genuinely need that much reach.
choices.explanation: Some do, but need and trust have to be judged for this particular task.

choices.text: Look for site-specific access or a narrower alternative, and check the publisher first.
choices.explanation: A broad grant reaches far beyond the task.

choices.text: Install it just for the one task and remove it straight afterwards; short use means no risk.
choices.explanation: An extension can read your data during that time.

questions.question: At a café, your bank’s page shows HTTPS. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The traffic to that host is encrypted; still verify the host and how you reached it.
choices.explanation: Encryption protects the traffic even on public Wi-Fi, but a scam site can use HTTPS too.

choices.text: Café Wi-Fi is always unsafe, so avoid your bank there even if the page shows HTTPS.
choices.explanation: That blanket claim does not reflect modern HTTPS guidance.

choices.text: HTTPS proves the page really belongs to your bank, not to someone imitating it.
choices.explanation: Encryption does not prove who runs the site.

questions.question: A family sets up filtering DNS on their home router. What limitation should they understand?

choices.text: It makes every device in the house safe from any phishing attempt, whether it comes by email, text or web.
choices.explanation: Unknown domains, apps and alternative resolvers can slip past the layer.

choices.text: It can block known bad domains, but cannot judge every scam or protect devices away from home.
choices.explanation: DNS filtering is a useful layer, not universal protection, and it only covers devices that use that resolver.

choices.text: It guarantees protection even when family phones are away from home on mobile data.
choices.explanation: The home router does not control traffic that leaves its network.

questions.question: After a login alert, you find a mail-forwarding rule you do not recognize. What should you do?

choices.text: Ignore the rule and the alert, since login alerts can be inaccurate and it is probably nothing.
choices.explanation: The rule needs investigating whatever the alert says.

choices.text: Assume the odd location in the login alert is enough on its own to prove someone broke into the account.
choices.explanation: Travel and network routing can distort location labels.

choices.text: Treat it as a warning: check the real account, remove anything unauthorized, review recent activity.
choices.explanation: A forwarding rule can expose future mail, so confirm who set it up before drawing conclusions.

questions.question: After a password-change alert, you cannot get into your email. Which recovery path is sensible?

choices.text: Open the provider’s own recovery page on a device you trust, not via the link in the alert.
choices.explanation: Starting from the provider’s own recovery page avoids the alert’s link, and a trusted device avoids a compromised machine; incognito mode alone does not clean a device.

choices.text: Tap the recovery link in the alert straight away, since acting fast matters more than checking who sent it.
choices.explanation: The alert itself may be phishing.

choices.text: Use an incognito window on your usual computer; that makes even an infected device safe.
choices.explanation: Private browsing does not remove malware.

questions.question: An attacker is in your inbox right now. As an individual, not an organization, what should you do?

choices.text: Quietly watch and screenshot everything the intruder does, so you have a full record of evidence before you act.
choices.explanation: Watching an active intruder can prolong the unauthorized access.

choices.text: Use the real service to remove forwarding and recovery changes, change the password and revoke sessions.
choices.explanation: Work through the real service or the provider’s recovery route: remove unauthorized forwarding and recovery changes, change the password and revoke sessions where supported, because containing active access comes before preserving whatever records are available.

choices.text: Reply to one of their emails, politely, to learn who they are and what they want.
choices.explanation: Replying may reveal more information without containing the access.

choices.text: Open your browser’s DevTools and monitor the inbox’s network traffic to see what the intruder is doing.
choices.explanation: Developer tools are not needed before basic account containment.

questions.question: A US resident discovers that a new credit account has been opened in their name. Which response fits the situation?

choices.text: Contact the issuer, get a plan at IdentityTheft.gov and consider freezing your credit.
choices.explanation: These are US-specific identity-theft tools, and the exact reports and disputes depend on the facts of the case.

choices.text: Follow a guide written for another country, since identity-theft steps are much the same everywhere.
choices.explanation: Credit reporting and legal routes differ by jurisdiction.

choices.text: Wait to see whether a second fraudulent account turns up, so you have more to report.
choices.explanation: Delay can allow additional misuse.

questions.question: Three months after a credential-stuffing incident on your email account, the single most useful follow-up action is:

choices.text: Create a new email address, migrate everything to it, and abandon the old one.
choices.explanation: A new address alone does not remove old unauthorized access.

choices.text: Wipe and reinstall the operating system on every device you own, to be sure nothing is left behind.
choices.explanation: Reinstalling every device is disproportionate without evidence that a device was compromised.

choices.text: Buy identity-theft insurance, so that any losses from the old incident are covered.
choices.explanation: Insurance does not inspect your account settings.

choices.text: Re-audit the email account’s sessions, forwarding rules, connected apps and recovery contacts.
choices.explanation: Reviewing sessions, forwarding, third-party app access, recovery details and available login history can catch lingering unauthorized settings, though not every past incident leaves one.
